439-Mile Survivor 1969 Hemi GTX Ragtop Breaks Cover at MCACN After 36 Years on Jackstands
26 photos
Photo: Facebook/Robert Carl
How is it possible that certain Hemi Mopars reach 2026 with fewer than 500 original miles on the clock, most of them accumulated in 1,320-foot increments? Here is one such unicorn, Mr. Motech’s 1969 Plymouth GTX “GTXterminator” ragtop race car. It just broke cover at the Muscle Car and Corvette Nationals, after a long 36-year spent on jack stands.
During the height of Detroit's horsepower wars, select 426-cubic-inch machines skipped daily street duty entirely. Purchased solely to conquer quarter-mile drag strips, they traveled from garage to racetrack on open trailers before slipping into quiet hibernation, preserving factory sheet metal and astonishingly low odometer readings across nearly 60 years.
One of the rarest examples of that phenomenon commanded attention during its unveiling at the 2026 Muscle Car and Corvette Nationals, documented by Geoff Stunkard on his YouTube channel, Geoff Stunkard's Zookeeper's Diary. This bright metallic blue 1969 Plymouth Hemi GTX convertible displays just 439 documented original miles. Originally owned and campaigned by John Tedder, it stands as one of only 11 U.S.-market 1969 Hemi GTX convertibles ever produced.
Tedder was far from an ordinary weekend racer; a prominent Chrysler insider known as "Mr. MoTech," he founded the MoTech program and once resolved a Maryland titling snag caused by bumperless Plymouth Superbirds. Ordered under the Tedder & Ulrich banner specifically to battle Chevrolets in NHRA Super Stock E Automatic and SS/FA competition, the GTX scored a class-winning ET of 11.86 seconds at 117.84 mph, recorded at the 1969 Winternationals.
Photo: Facebook/Robert Carl That was only the beginning; during a blistering 1970 campaign, Tedder's Hemi ragtop reigned as the top SS/EA contender in the nation, sweeping class victories at the 1970 Winternationals, the 1970 Gatornationals, and the 1970 Springnationals while also capturing Super Stock Eliminator Runner-Up honors at the Gatornationals.
Back then, the convertible cut an unmistakable profile at the starting line, painted blue across its nose and white along its tail, topped by a convertible roof painted black forward and white behind. Once its competitive career concluded, the Plymouth's survival became a saga of fortunate timing.
In 1983, a prospective buyer placed a $500 deposit and never returned, even though Tedder had already mailed the title. About a year later in the mid-1980s, Tedder phoned an enthusiast named Don, who had bought an identically configured 1969 440-cubic-inch 4-speed GTX convertible new. Don hooked an open trailer to a Dodge Dakota and hauled the 182-mile Hemi Mopar home.
Photo: Facebook/William Pearce An Air Force serviceman stationed in Shreveport, Louisiana, first encountered the convertible at a 1987 local Mopar club gathering, committing its details to memory. By 1990, Don placed the Plymouth onto jack stands, beginning an unbroken 36-year slumber.
Around 2014, while preparing to move back to Maryland, Tedder spotted the car's original 426-cubic-inch block—which had spun its number-one bearing decades earlier—resting beneath his workbench, phoned Don, and reunited the matching-numbers engine with its chassis.
Nearly 40 years after that Shreveport meeting, the former airman answered a Moparts wanted ad for space-saver wheels, recognized the Louisiana area code, and asked about Don. That chance conversation connected current owner Robert Carl and his mechanic to Don's family. Following a year of respectful negotiations, the family entrusted the GTX to Carl as its next caretaker, finally lowering the historic drag car off jack stands for the first time since 1990.
Photo: Facebook/Robert Carl Wisely resisting a full restoration, the new owner preserved the 439-mile survivor with all original sheet metal, its original fender tag, and its complete numbers-matching drivetrain intact under metallic blue paint and blue vinyl upholstery.
Awakening it required pulling the distributor, priming the oiling system, flushing stale fuel and fluids, adjusting the valvetrain, and replacing brittle convertible-top hydraulic lines. It’s probably one of the car’s rare top-down public appearances, since Tedder raced it roof-up.
That extraordinary survivor belongs to one of Detroit's most distinctive muscle car lineages. Debuting for 1967 as the upscale Belvedere GTX before standing alone from 1968 through 1971 , Plymouth's B-body flagship earned billing as the "gentleman's muscle car."
Photo: Facebook/Robert Carl Unlike stripped-down street brawlers, it paired bucket-seat comfort and heavy-duty suspension with a standard 440-cubic-inch, 375-horsepower Super Commando V8, leaving the 426-cube, 425-horsepower Street Hemi as its ultimate option before reverting to a Road Runner package through 1974.
Higher showroom pricing and internal competition from the wildly popular Road Runner kept GTX sales modest throughout its standalone run. Mother Mopar built 12,690 units in 1967, peaked at 18,940 in 1968, eased to 15,602 in 1969, tumbled to 7,748 in 1970, and closed at 2,942 in 1971. All in all, just 57,922 cars were sold.
GTX convertibles lasted just 3 years: 680 in 1967, 1,026 in 1968, and 700 in 1969. Specify the legendary Street Hemi, and those production figures shrink dramatically. Across all five standalone model years from 1967 through 1971, Plymouth produced just 1,490 Hemi GTXs combined.
Photo: Facebook/Robert Carl Yearly output declined steadily as insurance surcharges climbed and emissions rules tightened: 733 examples in 1967, 446 in 1968, 209 in 1969, 72 in 1970, and only 30 in 1971, closing the curtain on Chrysler's iconic 426-cubic-inch V8.
Breaking down 1969 production underscores how scarce Tedder's machine truly is. Of 15,602 GTXs assembled, 14,902 were two-door hardtops; 700 were convertibles, and comprised 689 440 models, plus 11 Hemis: four 4-speeds and seven automatics. This is one of those magnificent seven Torqueflite examples (the automatic was the preferred solution by drag racers).
In 1969, ordering a Hemi GTX convertible demanded real money. The convertible opened at $3,635—$219 above the $3,416 hardtop—and adding the 426 Hemi cost $656, lifting its base sticker to $4,291 before mandatory heavy-duty equipment.
Over the past five years, Hemi GTX convertibles sales yield a $166,375 median, while the record (for both a 1969 model and any Hemi GTX convertible) remains a $230,000 from a Mecum auction in 2017 ($253k with buyer’s fee). I wonder what this unicorn would go for, if it were for sale.
